## Setup and Data Loading

```{r}
#| include: false

# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(gt)

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Load the training and test datasets
ems_train <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("data", "processed", "ems_train.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

ems_test <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("data", "processed", "ems_test.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Check the structure of the training data
glimpse(ems_train)

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Check the training and test periods
ems_train |>
  summarise(
    First_Week = min(Week),
    Last_Week = max(Week),
    Weeks = n_distinct(Week)
  )

ems_test |>
  summarise(
    First_Week = min(Week),
    Last_Week = max(Week),
    Weeks = n_distinct(Week)
  )

```

## 1. Response-Time Trends

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Plot weekly response times by emergency category
ggplot(ems_train, aes(
  x = Week,
  y = Arrival_Seconds,
  color = Category
)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly EMS Response Times by Emergency Category",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Arrival Time (Seconds)",
    color = "Emergency Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

**Interpretation.** On average, response times were shorter for life-threatening incidents at 596 seconds while non-life-threatening incidents averaged 896 seconds. Non-life-threatening response times were also more variable.

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Calculate mean response time by category
ems_train |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarise(
    Mean_Arrival_Seconds = round(
      mean(Arrival_Seconds, na.rm = TRUE),
      2
    )
  )

```

## 2. Seasonality and Unusual Changes

```{r}
#| include: false

# Convert training data to a weekly time series (tsibble)
ems_train_ts <- ems_train |>
  as_tsibble(
    key = Category,
    index = Week
  )

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Examine seasonal patterns in arrival times
ems_train_ts |>
  gg_season(Arrival_Seconds, period = "year") +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern of EMS Response Times",
    y = "Arrival Time (Seconds)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Calculate trend and seasonal strength
stl_features <- ems_train_ts |>
  features(
    Arrival_Seconds,
    feat_stl,
    .period = 52
  )

stl_features |>
  select(
    Category,
    trend_strength,
    seasonal_strength_52
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))
  )

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Identify weeks with the highest response times
ems_train |>
  arrange(desc(Arrival_Seconds)) |>
  select(
    Week,
    Category,
    Arrival_Seconds,
    Incidents
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

```

**Interpretation.** Response times showed stronger long-term trends than seasonal patterns during the training period (2013–2025). Annual seasonal strength was 0.223 for life-threatening emergencies and 0.260 for non-life-threatening emergencies. Non-life-threatening incidents also experienced larger unusual response-time spikes, particularly during 2020.

## 3. Response-Time Forecasting Models

```{r}
#| include: false

# Convert test data to a weekly tsibble
ems_test_ts <- ems_test |>
  as_tsibble(
    key = Category,
    index = Week
  )

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Fit response-time forecasting models: Seasonal Naive, ETS and ARIMA
response_models <- ems_train_ts |>
  model(
    Seasonal_Naive = SNAIVE(Arrival_Seconds ~ lag("year")),
    ETS = ETS(Arrival_Seconds),
    ARIMA = ARIMA(Arrival_Seconds)
  )

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Forecasts response times for the 52-week test period
response_fc <- response_models |>
  forecast(new_data = ems_test_ts)

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Compare forecast model accuracy on the test data
response_accuracy <- response_fc |>
  accuracy(ems_test_ts) |>
  select(
    Category,
    .model,
    RMSE,
    MAE,
    MAPE
  ) |>
  arrange(Category, RMSE)

response_accuracy

```

### Manual ARIMA Model Selection

```{r}
# Check differencing requirements for each emergency category

ems_train_ts |>
  features(Arrival_Seconds, unitroot_ndiffs)

ems_train_ts |>
  features(Arrival_Seconds, unitroot_nsdiffs)
```

```{r}
# ACF and PACF: Life-Threatening emergencies

ems_train_ts |>
  filter(Category == "Life-Threatening") |>
  mutate(
    diff_arrival = difference(Arrival_Seconds)
  ) |>
  gg_tsdisplay(
    diff_arrival,
    plot_type = "partial"
  )
```

```{r}
# ACF and PACF: Non-Life-Threatening emergencies

ems_train_ts |>
  filter(Category == "Non-Life-Threatening") |>
  mutate(
    diff_arrival = difference(Arrival_Seconds)
  ) |>
  gg_tsdisplay(
    diff_arrival,
    plot_type = "partial"
  )
```

```{r}
# Manual versus automatic ARIMA model comparison
# Models fitted using training data only

manual_response_fit <- ems_train_ts |>
  model(
    ARIMA_011 = ARIMA(Arrival_Seconds ~ pdq(0, 1, 1)),
    ARIMA_012 = ARIMA(Arrival_Seconds ~ pdq(0, 1, 2)),
    Auto_ARIMA = ARIMA(Arrival_Seconds),
    ETS = ETS(Arrival_Seconds)
  )

# Compare model fit using training-data AICc
manual_response_fit |>
  glance() |>
  select(Category, .model, AICc) |>
  arrange(Category, AICc)
```

```{r}
# Evaluate manual ARIMA, automatic ARIMA, and ETS
# Using the same 52-week test period

manual_response_fc <- manual_response_fit |>
  forecast(new_data = ems_test_ts)

manual_response_accuracy <- manual_response_fc |>
  accuracy(ems_test_ts) |>
  select(Category, .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  arrange(Category, RMSE)

manual_response_accuracy
```

### Manual vs. Automatic ARIMA Interpretation

Manual ARIMA models were selected using differencing tests and the ACF/PACF patterns of the training series. Both emergency categories suggested one regular difference and no seasonal difference. ARIMA(0,1,1) and ARIMA(0,1,2) were compared with automatically selected ARIMA and ETS models using the same 52-week test period.

ETS achieved the lowest RMSE and MAE for both emergency categories. However, manually selected ARIMA(0,1,1) achieved the lowest MAPE, with 8.37% for life-threatening emergencies and 19.02% for non-life-threatening emergencies. Manual ARIMA(0,1,1) also outperformed automatic ARIMA across all three test accuracy metrics.

Although automatic ARIMA had the lowest AICc among the ARIMA candidates on the training data, it produced higher test-set errors than the manually selected ARIMA(0,1,1) model. These findings demonstrate that automatically selected models do not always provide the most accurate forecasts on unseen data, and model selection depends partly on the evaluation metric.

```{r}
#| echo: false

# ETS forecasts of EMS Response Times
ets_fc <- response_fc |>
  filter(.model == "ETS")

# Show recent history, ETS forecasts, and actual test values
ets_fc |>
  autoplot(
    ems_train_ts |>
      filter(Week >= as.Date("2023-01-01")),
    level = c(80, 95)
  ) +
  autolayer(
    ems_test_ts,
    Arrival_Seconds,
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ Category,
    scales = "free_y",
    ncol = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "ETS Forecasts of EMS Response Times",
    subtitle = "Forecasts compared with actual response times in the 52-week test period",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Arrival Time (Seconds)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

**Interpretation.** ETS achieved the lowest RMSE and MAE for both emergency categories in the expanded model comparison. However, manual ARIMA(0,1,1) achieved slightly lower MAPE. Both models forecasted life-threatening response times more accurately than non-life-threatening response times.

```{r}
# Check residuals for ETS and ARIMA models
# ETS residual diagnostics: Life-Threatening emergencies

response_models |>
  filter(Category == "Life-Threatening") |>
  select(ETS) |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

```{r}
# ETS residual diagnostics: Non-Life-Threatening emergencies

response_models |>
  filter(Category == "Non-Life-Threatening") |>
  select(ETS) |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

```{r}
# ARIMA residual diagnostics: Life-Threatening emergencies

response_models |>
  filter(Category == "Life-Threatening") |>
  select(ARIMA) |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

```{r}
# ARIMA residual diagnostics: Non-Life-Threatening emergencies

response_models |>
  filter(Category == "Non-Life-Threatening") |>
  select(ARIMA) |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

```{r}
# Ljung-Box test for response-time model residuals

response_models |>
  select(ETS, ARIMA) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 20)
```

### Residual Diagnostics Interpretation

The Ljung–Box test was conducted at lag 20 to evaluate residual autocorrelation. ARIMA showed no statistically significant remaining autocorrelation for either life-threatening (p = 0.966) or non-life-threatening (p = 0.996) emergencies. In contrast, ETS showed significant remaining autocorrelation for both life-threatening (p = 0.031) and non-life-threatening (p = 0.041) emergencies.

Although automatically selected ARIMA demonstrated more favorable residual diagnostics, ETS achieved lower RMSE and MAE on the 52-week test set. Manual ARIMA(0,1,1) achieved slightly lower MAPE than ETS. These findings suggest that model selection should consider forecast accuracy, the evaluation metric, and residual diagnostics rather than relying on a single measure.

## 3.1. Rolling-Origin Cross-Validation

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Run rolling-origin cross-validation for the ETS model
response_cv <- ems_train_ts |>
  stretch_tsibble(
    .init = 260,
    .step = 13
  )

response_cv_fit <- response_cv |>
  model(
    ETS = ETS(Arrival_Seconds)
  )

response_cv_fc <- response_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

response_cv_accuracy <- response_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(
    ems_train_ts,
    by = c("Category", ".model")
  ) |>
  select(Category, .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE)

response_cv_accuracy

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Calculate forecast errors for each CV period
response_cv_results <- response_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(
    ems_train_ts |>
      as_tibble() |>
      select(
        Week,
        Category,
        Actual = Arrival_Seconds
      ),
    by = c("Week", "Category")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Error = Actual - .mean,
    Absolute_Error = abs(Error),
    APE = abs(Error / Actual) * 100
  )

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Keep valid cross-validation results
response_cv_results_valid <- response_cv_results |>
  filter(
    !is.na(Actual),
    is.finite(APE)
  )

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Plot rolling-origin forecast errors over time
response_cv_results_valid |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Week, y = APE, color = Category)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ Category,
    ncol = 1,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Rolling-Origin Cross-Validation of EMS Response Times",
    subtitle = "One-week-ahead ETS forecast errors across 28 forecast periods",
    x = "Forecast Week",
    y = "Absolute Percentage Error (%)",
    color = "Emergency Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )

```

**Interpretation.** Rolling-origin validation showed that ETS performed well across different periods. Forecast errors stayed low for life-threatening incidents with a MAPE of 3.19% compared to 7.38%.

## 3.2 Full History vs. Recent Training Window

```{r}
#| include: false

# Create the 2022-onward training dataset
response_train_recent <- ems_train_ts |>
  filter(Week >= as.Date("2022-01-01"))

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Fit ETS using the recent training period
response_recent_fit <- response_train_recent |>
  model(
    ETS = ETS(Arrival_Seconds)
  )

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Forecast the test period using the recent-history ETS model
response_recent_fc <- response_recent_fit |>
  forecast(new_data = ems_test_ts)

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Calculate recent-history ETS forecast accuracy
response_recent_accuracy <- response_recent_fc |>
  accuracy(ems_test_ts) |>
  select(Category, .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE)

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Compare full-history and recent-history ETS accuracy
response_window_accuracy <- bind_rows(
  response_accuracy |>
    filter(.model == "ETS") |>
    mutate(Training_Window = "Full History (2013-2025)"),
  
  response_recent_accuracy |>
    mutate(Training_Window = "Recent History (2022-2025)")
) |>
  select(
    Category,
    Training_Window,
    RMSE,
    MAE,
    MAPE
  )

response_window_accuracy |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "ETS Response-Time Accuracy by Training Window",
    subtitle = "Life-Threatening vs. Non-Life-Threatening EMS Incidents"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Category = "Emergency Category",
    Training_Window = "Training Window",
    RMSE = "RMSE",
    MAE = "MAE",
    MAPE = "MAPE"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(RMSE, MAE),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = MAPE,
    decimals = 2,
    pattern = "{x}%"
  ) |>
  cols_align(
    align = "center",
    columns = everything()
  )

```

**Interpretation.** Full-history training produced lower RMSE for both emergency categories. However, recent-history training slightly improved MAPE for non-life-threatening emergencies (18.79% versus 19.79%). Overall, the results were mixed, with no consistent advantage from using only recent data.

### 3.3 ARIMA Hyperparameter Tuning for EMS Response Times

To systematically evaluate ARIMA configurations for EMS response-time forecasting, we tested nine combinations of autoregressive (p) and moving-average (q) orders for both life-threatening and non-life-threatening emergencies.

Based on the earlier differencing analysis, we fixed d = 1 and used nonseasonal models without drift. Each configuration was evaluated using rolling-origin cross-validation with an initial training window of 260 weeks, a step size of 13 weeks, and one-week-ahead forecasts.

RMSE was used as the primary selection metric, with MAE and MAPE included for additional comparison. All tuning was conducted using the training data, without using the original 52-week test period.

```{r}

# Rolling-origin cross-validation for both response categories
response_tuning_cv <- ems_train_ts |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 260, .step = 13)

# Test nine ARIMA configurations
response_arima_models <- response_tuning_cv |>
  model(
    ARIMA_010 = ARIMA(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ 0 + pdq(0,1,0) + PDQ(0,0,0)
    ),
    ARIMA_011 = ARIMA(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ 0 + pdq(0,1,1) + PDQ(0,0,0)
    ),
    ARIMA_012 = ARIMA(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ 0 + pdq(0,1,2) + PDQ(0,0,0)
    ),
    ARIMA_110 = ARIMA(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ 0 + pdq(1,1,0) + PDQ(0,0,0)
    ),
    ARIMA_111 = ARIMA(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ 0 + pdq(1,1,1) + PDQ(0,0,0)
    ),
    ARIMA_112 = ARIMA(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ 0 + pdq(1,1,2) + PDQ(0,0,0)
    ),
    ARIMA_210 = ARIMA(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ 0 + pdq(2,1,0) + PDQ(0,0,0)
    ),
    ARIMA_211 = ARIMA(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ 0 + pdq(2,1,1) + PDQ(0,0,0)
    ),
    ARIMA_212 = ARIMA(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ 0 + pdq(2,1,2) + PDQ(0,0,0)
    )
  )

# Forecast one week ahead
response_arima_fc <- response_arima_models |>
  forecast(h = 1)

# Compare models using RMSE, MAE, and MAPE
response_arima_accuracy <- response_arima_fc |>
  accuracy(ems_train_ts) |>
  select(Category, .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  arrange(Category, RMSE)

response_arima_accuracy

# Find the best ARIMA model for each response category
response_arima_best <- response_arima_accuracy |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  slice_min(RMSE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

response_arima_best

```

### 3.4 ETS Configuration Tuning for EMS Response Times

To evaluate whether alternative exponential smoothing configurations could improve EMS response-time forecasts, we compared six nonseasonal ETS configurations and automatically selected ETS for both emergency categories.

The configurations varied their error and trend components while holding seasonality at none, consistent with the relatively weak seasonal patterns observed in the earlier analysis.

All models were evaluated using rolling-origin cross-validation with an initial training window of 260 weeks, a step size of 13 weeks, and one-week-ahead forecasts. RMSE was the primary selection metric, with MAE and MAPE included as supporting measures. Only training-period observations were used.

```{r}

# Create rolling-origin cross-validation windows
# for both emergency categories

response_ets_cv <- ems_train_ts |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 260, .step = 13)

# Fit six ETS configurations plus automatic ETS
response_ets_models <- response_ets_cv |>
  model(
    ETS_ANN = ETS(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ error("A") + trend("N") + season("N")
    ),
    
    ETS_AAN = ETS(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("N")
    ),
    
    ETS_AAdN = ETS(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("N")
    ),
    
    ETS_MNN = ETS(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ error("M") + trend("N") + season("N")
    ),
    
    ETS_MAN = ETS(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ error("M") + trend("A") + season("N")
    ),
    
    ETS_MAdN = ETS(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ error("M") + trend("Ad") + season("N")
    ),
    
    ETS_Auto = ETS(Arrival_Seconds)
  )

# Forecast one week ahead
response_ets_fc <- response_ets_models |>
  forecast(h = 1)

# Compare ETS forecast accuracy
response_ets_accuracy <- response_ets_fc |>
  accuracy(ems_train_ts) |>
  select(Category, .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  arrange(Category, RMSE)

response_ets_accuracy

# Identify the best ETS configuration for each category
response_ets_best <- response_ets_accuracy |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  slice_min(RMSE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

response_ets_best

```

### 3.5 Multi-Horizon Response-Time Model Validation

To assess how forecasting performance changes over longer planning periods, we compared four candidate models across both emergency categories: ARIMA(1,1,1), ARIMA(2,1,0), ETS(A,N,N), and automatically selected ETS.

Rolling-origin cross-validation was conducted using an initial training window of 260 weeks and a step size of 26 weeks. Each model generated forecasts up to 52 weeks ahead.

Accuracy was evaluated at forecast horizons of 1, 4, 12, and 52 weeks. We also calculated accuracy across the complete 52-week forecast windows, using RMSE as the primary model selection metric. Only training-period observations were used in this experiment.

```{r}

# Create rolling-origin windows for both response categories
response_horizon_cv <- ems_train_ts |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 260, .step = 26)

# Fit four shortlisted forecasting models
response_horizon_models <- response_horizon_cv |>
  model(
    ARIMA_111 = ARIMA(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ 0 + pdq(1,1,1) + PDQ(0,0,0)
    ),
    ARIMA_210 = ARIMA(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ 0 + pdq(2,1,0) + PDQ(0,0,0)
    ),
    ETS_ANN = ETS(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ error("A") + trend("N") + season("N")
    ),
    ETS_Auto = ETS(Arrival_Seconds)
  )

# Generate forecasts up to 52 weeks ahead
response_horizon_fc <- response_horizon_models |>
  forecast(h = 52)

# Identify the forecast horizon for each prediction
response_horizon_predictions <- response_horizon_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(Category, .model, .id) |>
  arrange(Week, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(Horizon = row_number()) |>
  ungroup()

# Match predictions with actual training-period observations
response_horizon_actuals <- ems_train_ts |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Category, Week, Actual = Arrival_Seconds)

response_horizon_errors <- response_horizon_predictions |>
  inner_join(
    response_horizon_actuals,
    by = c("Category", "Week")
  ) |>
  group_by(Category, .model, .id) |>
  filter(n() == 52) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    Error = Actual - .mean,
    Absolute_Error = abs(Error),
    APE = abs(Error / Actual) * 100
  )

# Compare accuracy at four forecast horizons
response_horizon_accuracy <- response_horizon_errors |>
  filter(Horizon %in% c(1, 4, 12, 52)) |>
  group_by(Category, Horizon, .model) |>
  summarise(
    RMSE = sqrt(mean(Error^2)),
    MAE = mean(Absolute_Error),
    MAPE = mean(APE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(Category, Horizon, RMSE)

response_horizon_accuracy

# Identify the best model at each horizon
response_horizon_winners <- response_horizon_accuracy |>
  group_by(Category, Horizon) |>
  slice_min(RMSE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

response_horizon_winners

# Evaluate accuracy across all 52 forecast weeks
response_full_horizon_accuracy <- response_horizon_errors |>
  group_by(Category, .model) |>
  summarise(
    RMSE = sqrt(mean(Error^2)),
    MAE = mean(Absolute_Error),
    MAPE = mean(APE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(Category, RMSE)

response_full_horizon_accuracy

# Select the best overall model for each category
response_full_horizon_winners <- response_full_horizon_accuracy |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  slice_min(RMSE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

response_full_horizon_winners

```

### Multi-Horizon Validation Interpretation

The multi-horizon analysis compared four forecasting models using rolling-origin cross-validation over complete 52-week forecast windows. For life-threatening emergencies, ARIMA(1,1,1) achieved the lowest overall RMSE of 48.77 seconds, with a MAE of 32.11 seconds and MAPE of 4.97%.

For non-life-threatening emergencies, ETS(A,N,N) achieved the lowest overall RMSE of 190.62 seconds, with a MAE of 121.62 seconds and MAPE of 12.47%. For non-life-threatening incidents, fixed and automatic ETS had nearly identical RMSE across the complete 52-week validation windows.

The results also showed that the best-performing model varied by forecast horizon. Although ARIMA performed better in the initial one-week-ahead tuning comparisons, ETS(A,N,N) provided the lowest overall error for non-life-threatening emergencies across the complete 52-week horizon.

The final model selections were based on RMSE across the complete 52-week cross-validation windows. These comparisons used an initial training window of 260 weeks and a step size of 26 weeks. The results should be interpreted as estimates of forecasting performance rather than definitive rankings.

## 4. Incident Counts and Response Times

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Plot the relationship between incident volume and response time
ggplot(
  ems_train,
  aes(
    x = Incidents,
    y = Arrival_Seconds,
    color = Category
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ Category,
    scales = "free"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Incident Counts and EMS Response Times",
    subtitle = "Weekly observations from the training period",
    x = "Weekly Incident Count",
    y = "Arrival Time (Seconds)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Calculate the correlation by emergency category
incident_correlations <- ems_train |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarise(
    Correlation = cor(
      Incidents,
      Arrival_Seconds,
      use = "complete.obs"
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Correlation = round(Correlation, 3)
  )

incident_correlations

```

**Interpretation.** Higher incident volume was associated with longer response times for life-threatening incidents (r = 0.501). The relationship was weaker for non-life-threatening incidents (r = 0.233).

### Dispatch and Travel Times for Two Similarly Busy Weeks

```{r}
ems_test |>
  filter(
    Category == "Non-Life-Threatening",
    Week %in% as.Date(c("2026-01-12", "2026-06-29"))
  ) |>
  arrange(Week) |>
  transmute(
    `Week starting` = Week,
    Incidents,
    `Call to arrival (min)` = Arrival_Seconds / 60,
    `Dispatch (min)` = Dispatch_Minutes,
    `Travel (min)` = Travel_Minutes
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = Incidents, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(`Call to arrival (min)`, `Dispatch (min)`, `Travel (min)`),
    decimals = 2
  )
```

The two weeks differed by only 34 non-life-threatening incidents, yet average call-to-arrival time was about 24 minutes longer in the week of June 29. Reported average dispatch time was 20.47 minutes higher, while average travel time was 3.18 minutes higher. The larger difference in dispatch time points to a stage worth investigating. The two-week comparison leaves open why dispatch took longer.

## 5. Future EMS Response-Time Forecasts

```{r}
# Prepare all available response-time data
# Combine training and testing observations

response_full <- bind_rows(ems_train, ems_test) |>
  arrange(Category, Week) |>
  select(Week, Category, Arrival_Seconds) |>
  as_tsibble(key = Category, index = Week)


# Refit selected models using all available historical data

# Life-threatening: ARIMA(1,1,1)
future_life_response_models <- response_full |>
  filter(Category == "Life-Threatening") |>
  model(
    ARIMA_111 = ARIMA(
      Arrival_Seconds ~ 0 + pdq(1,1,1) + PDQ(0,0,0)
    )
  )

# Non-life-threatening: ETS(A,N,N)
future_ntl_response_models <- response_full |>
  filter(Category == "Non-Life-Threatening") |>
  model(
    ETS_ANN = ETS(
      Arrival_Seconds ~
        error("A") + trend("N") + season("N")
    )
  )

# Generate 52-week forecasts from the selected models
future_life_response_fc <- future_life_response_models |>
  forecast(h = 52, level = c(80, 95))

future_ntl_response_fc <- future_ntl_response_models |>
  forecast(h = 52, level = c(80, 95))

# Combine the forecasts for both categories
future_response_fc <- bind_rows(
  future_life_response_fc,
  future_ntl_response_fc
)

# Display the first four forecast weeks for each category
future_response_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  slice_head(n = 4) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(Forecast_Minutes = .mean / 60) |>
  select(
    Week,
    Category,
    Forecast_Seconds = .mean,
    Forecast_Minutes
  )

```

```{r}
# Future EMS response-time forecasts
# Display historical observations and 80%/95% prediction intervals

future_response_fc |>
  autoplot(
    response_full |> filter_index("2024 Jan" ~ .),
    level = c(80, 95)
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Category, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "NYC EMS Response-Time Forecasts: 52 Weeks Ahead",
    subtitle = "Selected ARIMA and ETS models with 80% and 95% prediction intervals",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Average Call-to-Arrival Time (Seconds)"
  )
```

### Future Response-Time Forecast Interpretation

Using all available observations through September 14, 2026, the selected ARIMA(1,1,1) model forecasted an initial average call-to-arrival time of approximately 15.18 minutes for life-threatening emergencies. The forecast gradually decreased over the first several weeks before stabilizing.

For non-life-threatening emergencies, the selected ETS(A,N,N) model forecasted an average call-to-arrival time of approximately 40.63 minutes, remaining constant throughout the 52-week forecast horizon.

Both models produced widening 80% and 95% prediction intervals, indicating increasing uncertainty over longer forecasting periods. These forecasts reflect the elevated response times observed toward the end of the historical period.

Overall, the results suggest that response-time pressures may remain substantial, particularly for non-life-threatening incidents. The forecasts can support operational planning but should not be treated as exact predictions, since staffing, dispatch operations, and unexpected events could affect actual response times.

## 6. Response-Time Results

Life-threatening emergencies generally experienced shorter and more consistent response times than non-life-threatening emergencies.

In the initial 52-week test-set evaluation, automatically selected ETS achieved the lowest RMSE and MAE for both categories, while manually selected ARIMA(0,1,1) achieved slightly lower MAPE. Subsequent systematic tuning and multi-horizon cross-validation provided additional evidence for selecting different models based on the intended forecasting period.

Across the complete 52-week cross-validation windows, ARIMA(1,1,1) achieved the lowest RMSE of 48.77 seconds for life-threatening emergencies. ETS(A,N,N) achieved the lowest RMSE of 190.62 seconds for non-life-threatening emergencies. These models were selected from the four configurations evaluated in the multi-horizon experiment.

After refitting the selected models using all available historical data through September 14, 2026, the initial forecasts were approximately 15.18 minutes for life-threatening incidents and 40.63 minutes for non-life-threatening incidents.

The life-threatening forecast gradually decreased before stabilizing, while the non-life-threatening forecast remained relatively constant. Prediction intervals widened over the 52-week horizon, indicating increasing forecast uncertainty.

The results highlight persistent response-time pressures, particularly for non-life-threatening incidents. These forecasts may help support EMS planning, but the uncertainty and historical variability should be considered when interpreting longer-term predictions.
